Lưu Sắc Kim Hoàng là chiến dịch truyền t: Luu Sac Kim Hoang is a cultural communications campaign honoring the revival of Kim Hoang folk paintings — a traditional art form deeply rooted in Hanoi's artistic and cultural heritage.
Ra đời vào nửa sau thế kỷ XVIII tại làng: Originating in the second half of the 18th century in Kim Hoang village, Hoai Duc, Hanoi, Kim Hoang paintings were renowned for their signature vermilion-red paper, delicate woodblock carvings, and expressive color palette. Yet amid historical upheavals and the passage of time, this folk tradition nearly faded into oblivion.
Từ câu chuyện ấy, Lưu Sắc Kim Hoàng ra đ: Born from that story, Luu Sac Kim Hoang sets out to chronicle the revival journey while recognizing and honoring the artisans, researchers, and individuals who devoted themselves to safeguarding Kim Hoang art. Through storytelling, exhibitions, and hands-on experiences, the campaign invites the public to discover the beauty of Kim Hoang paintings and rekindle a lasting love for traditional Vietnamese folk art.
Góp phần đưa tranh dân gian Kim Hoàng đế: Bringing Kim Hoang folk paintings closer to the public; serving as a bridge between heritage custodians and folk art enthusiasts, fostering appreciation, contemporary creativity, and the continuity of Kim Hoang artistic values in modern life.
Lan tỏa câu chuyện về quá trình khôi phụ: Share the story of restoring Kim Hoang folk paintings and the timeless artistic values preserved across generations.
Bày tỏ sự trân trọng và biết ơn đến các: Pay tribute to the artisans, researchers, and dedicated individuals who poured their hearts and efforts into reviving and preserving this craft.
Tạo cơ hội để mọi người tìm hiểu, khám p: Create opportunities for everyone to learn, explore, and directly experience the art of Kim Hoang folk painting.
Khơi dậy tình yêu đối với nghệ thuật tru: Inspire a love for traditional art and encourage younger generations to care for, preserve, and share Kim Hoang heritage in contemporary life.

From surviving archives and traces, she brought together scholars, artisans, and painters to verify and restore a nearly lost artistic heritage.

Nguồn Cội Phường Tranh Kim Hoàng: Origins of the Kim Hoang Painting Guild
Kim Hoàng là một làng ven đô, phía tây t: Kim Hoang was a village on the outskirts of the ancient city of Thang Long, to its west (now part of Son Dong Commune, Hanoi). According to the book Do Hoa Co Viet Nam (Ancient Vietnamese Graphics), in the 22nd year of the Chính Hòa reign (1701), the people of Kim Bang and Hoang Bang villages migrated from Thanh Hoa to the North and merged to form Kim Hoang village.
Theo đó, nhận thấy tranh Đông Hồ chỉ đủ: Recognizing that Dong Ho paintings could only meet the demand in areas such as Ha Bac, Hai Duong and Nam Dinh; Hang Trong paintings primarily served Hanoi and were unsuitable for farmers in terms of both aesthetics and affordability, the people of Kim Hoang, led by the Nguyen Sy and Nguyen The families, set out to create a new genre of folk painting that combined the techniques of both Dong Ho and Hang Trong. Gradually, the production of Kim Hoang paintings was organized into a “painting guild”, drawing the entire village into the trade.
Hàng năm vào rằm tháng Giêng, người làng: Every year, on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, the people of Kim Hoang began their annual painting season. The paintings were produced using woodblocks. These blocks were kept by the guild master, who was skilled in both drawing and carving. During the printing process, families exchanged woodblocks with one another. At the end of the season, all the blocks were returned to the guild master.
Vào những ngày giáp Tết xưa, không khí l: In the days leading up to Tet, the village was once filled with the bustling atmosphere of painting production. Everyone worked tirelessly throughout the day and night, and when evening came, they would light oil lamps to apply colours to the prints. After nearly a year of preparation, around the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month, the paintings were taken to markets in the surrounding areas for sale. Early in the morning, each painting-making household would send someone to the local markets to “reserve a spot with a stick”. Only when daylight broke would other family members carry bundles of paintings to set up their stalls and sell them individually to local people preparing for the Lunar New Year. Kim Hoàng paintings were carried to markets such as Sau Gia, Son Đong, Chua Thay, Canh and Dien. According to the recollections of the village elders, in prosperous years, a person returning from the market after selling paintings would carry a shoulder pole heavily laden with Tu Duc copper coins.
Cụ Trần Sơn Phương lại có những ký ức ri: Elder Tran Son Phuong, however, had his own distinct memories of the painting trade in Kim Hoang: “My father made a living as a painting merchant. Every Tet, he would go to collect paintings and sell them throughout the surrounding areas. Regularly, as evening fell, he would visit familiar suppliers to collect the paintings, tie them securely into bundles, and then set off early the next morning to sell them at markets in the area. Back then, trading was simple, yet full of joy. Kim Hoang paintings were an indispensable item in every household during Tet, so whatever quantity my father collected each day, he would sell out by the end of that day. When he returned home in the afternoon, the load on his shoulders was almost weightless. My siblings and I would run after him excitedly, begging him to let us hang from the carrying pole's ropes…”
Tết Hà Nội 1896, chụp bởi Andres Salles: Hanoi Tet 1896, photographed by Andres Salles
Đến năm Ất Mão đời Duy Tân (1915), xảy r: In the year At Mao, during the reign of Duy Tan (1915), a major flood occurred when the Lien Mac dike broke, inundating a vast area west of Hanoi and sweeping away the woodblock storage of the Kim Hoang painting guild. From then on, the Kim Hoang painting trade began to decline. Only a handful of households remained, reluctant to part with their painting blocks, and tried to preserve them in order to keep the craft alive.
Thêm vào đó, về sau thị hiếu người dân c: In addition, as people's tastes gradually shifted towards Hang Trong paintings, the people of Kim Hoang began purchasing Hang Trong paintings to resell in the surrounding rural villages. As a result, the market for Kim Hoang paintings gradually shrank. At first, a few households in Kim Hoang still tried to hold on to the trade, driven by hope and lingering attachment to the craft.
Đến năm 1945 khi cuộc chiến chống Pháp b: By 1945, when the resistance war against the French began, the impact of war, famine and increasingly difficult living conditions forced the remaining woodblocks to be sold. The custom of displaying folk paintings during Tet also gradually faded over time, causing the village's printing trade to fall apart. “By around the late 1950s, the campaign against superstitious practices led to the remaining woodblocks being chopped up for firewood,” recalled Tran At, the oldest person in the village. And so, Kim Hoang lost an entire genre of folk painting…
Tư liệu TTXVN, tổng hợp bởi báo Nhân Dân: VNA Archive, compiled by Nhan Dan Newspaper
Tưởng chừng số phận dòng tranh Kim Hoàng: It seemed that the fate of the Kim Hoang painting tradition had been forgotten. However, the French researcher Maurice Durand had collected ancestral worship paintings and Tet paintings from Northern Vietnam and preserved them at the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient (EFEO), among which were several original Kim Hoang paintings. In 1960, Maurice Durand's book Tranh dan gian Viet Nam (L'imagerie populaire Vietnamienne) was published. Besides the two famous painting traditions of Hang Trong and Dong Ho, Durand also introduced several other paintings without specifying their origins. It was only after many years of searching that the Vietnam Fine Arts Museum eventually traced these paintings back to Kim Hoang village, right at the gateway to the capital city of Hanoi.
Các cụ cao tuổi ở làng Kim Hoàng khi xem: When the elderly villagers of Kim Hoang looked through M. Durand's book, they too recognized the familiar paintings of their village. Although these were only black-and-white photographs, they seemed to evoke the hues of the red paintings of years gone by. And so, the Kim Hoang folk painting tradition officially entered the history of fine arts research in Vietnam.
Đến năm 2011, sự may mắn đã đến với công: In 2011, a stroke of good fortune came to the efforts to collect and restore Kim Hoang paintings when the French School of the Far East (EFEO) republished Tranh dan gian Viet Nam, this time featuring colour illustrations of folk paintings. Based on examinations of colours, lines and artistic styles, researchers identified 58 Kim Hoang folk paintings among them. This became an important source of reference, opening up possibilities for researching and reconstructing the Kim Hoang painting tradition with its distinctive red background.
Đến khoảng năm 2013, hai cụ cao niên làn: Around 2013, two elderly villagers from Kim Hoang travelled to Dong Ho painting village to seek assistance in restoring the woodblocks, but their efforts were unsuccessful.

Không cam tâm để dòng tranh này chỉ còn: Unwilling to accept that this painting tradition should exist only in a few brief lines on the pages of books, antique art collector Nguyen Thi Thu Hoa (Director of the Hanoi Museum of Ceramics) travelled to Kim Hoang village to speak with its elderly residents. In 2015, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Hoa officially initiated a project to revive Kim Hoang folk paintings. She was determined to restore the Kim Hoang folk painting tradition and bring it back into contemporary life. “But of course, it sounds wonderful when put into words, but the work is extremely difficult and exhausting.” To revive a painting tradition that had been lost, historical documents alone were not enough. It also required research into printing techniques, colours, paper materials, painting methods, as well as the involvement of artisans knowledgeable in Vietnamese folk painting and artists experienced in woodblock printing.
Ý thức được hành trình gian nan phía trư: Aware of the arduous journey ahead, Thu Hoa proactively sought out and brought together a team of leading experts, researchers and artisans to work towards this common goal. She shared: “To revive this painting tradition, we needed a very large team working alongside one another. This is because the work does not stop at tracing its origins; it also requires the meticulous reconstruction of every stage of the process: from researching colours and paper materials, to printing methods, colouring techniques and even the techniques used to dry the paintings.”
Tiến sĩ Nguyễn Thị Thu Hòa, chụp bởi afa: Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Hoa, photo by afamily.vn
Phần 5 • Khôi Phục Sắc Màu, Mộc Bản, Giấ: Part 5 • Restoring Colors, Woodblocks, Do Paper & New Motifs
Dự án nhanh chóng nhận được sự chung tay: The project quickly received the support and contributions of many renowned researchers and artisans. While researcher Tran Hau Yen The and calligrapher Le Quoc Viet compared historical materials to restore the distinctive artistic characteristics of the paintings, traditional artisans contributed their expertise in technical aspects: artisan Nguyen Dang Che (Dong Ho) shared his knowledge of paper dyeing, artisan Nguyen Dang Tam (Dong Ho) took part in woodblock carving, and artisan Le Dinh Nghien (Hang Trong) provided guidance on traditional hand-colouring techniques. The responsibility for recreating and expanding the range of painting designs was entrusted to two artists, Nguyen Duc Hoa and Duc Phuong. Together, they brought exemplary paintings such as Than ke and Lon doc back to life through woodblock carving, painting and printing techniques that created raised forms. In particular, alongside restoring the traditional designs, artist Nguyen Duc Hoa also created new painting designs that inherited the artistic essence of Kim Hoang, breathing new life into the painting tradition in contemporary society.
Bước đầu, để xác định màu tranh được sử: At the initial stage, even determining the colours used in the paintings proved to be a challenging process. Based on Maurice Durand's book, the research team identified the colours as orange-red and canary yellow. However, as the colours in the collection may have faded over time, artist Nguyen Duc Hoa experimented with mixing different shades of orange. On the other hand, according to documents by various previous researchers, Kim Hoang folk paintings were printed on a type of paper known as "tau vang", although its exact nature has yet to be identified. The researchers hypothesized that, in order to keep production costs low and make the paintings accessible to the wider population, particularly farming households, the materials used to produce the colours may have been sourced from common materials readily available in the local area, such as the writing paper used by scholars of old.

Công việc không dừng ở việc làm ra những: The work did not stop at producing paintings that closely resembled the original designs. The woodblocks had to be restored or recreated; the printed lines needed to retain their original character; the colours had to reflect the distinctive characteristics of the painting tradition; and the colouring techniques needed to be flexible enough for each work to retain its own individual nuances. It was a process that involved research, practice and verification, in which knowledge drawn from historical materials had to be translated into the practical skills of the artisans.
Từ nỗ lực ấy, những mẫu tranh Kim Hoàng: Through these efforts, Kim Hoang painting designs gradually returned. The project successfully restored 33 woodblock-printed designs and 19 hand-painted designs. These figures demonstrate the tangible results of the restoration process, while also providing a foundation for further research, introduction and practice of the painting tradition in contemporary life.
Một dòng tranh chỉ thực sự có cơ hội sốn: A painting tradition can only truly have a chance of surviving when there are people who master its techniques, have the means to practise the craft and find economic and cultural value in their work. Therefore, rather than simply restoring paintings for preservation in museums, the project aimed to pass on these skills to local people. Artisan Dao Dinh Chung, a resident of Kim Hoang village, was supported in learning the various stages of woodblock carving, colour mixing, printing and painting completion. Since 2019, he has been able to make a living independently from the Kim Hoang painting trade, without requiring further financial support from the project. This is a noteworthy sign: conservation efforts have begun to create livelihoods, enabling those who practise traditional culture to continue their craft through their own abilities.
Phần 7 • Sức Sống Mới Của Tranh Dân Gian: Part 7 • New Vitality of Kim Hoang Folk Paintings in Contemporary Life
Tính đến nay đã gần 10 năm kể từ khi tra: Nearly ten years have now passed since Kim Hoang paintings were officially revived. Although the project has come to an end, the Kim Hoang folk painting tradition continues to develop. Artisan Chung remains dedicated to painting, while also actively participating in communications activities to promote this folk painting tradition and help it reach a wider audience. Alongside the traditional designs painted by artisans, young people today are also actively incorporating Kim Hoang folk paintings into modern materials and applications that are highly practical and more accessible in contemporary life. From technology and fashion to education, Kim Hoang folk paintings are now being adapted in flexible and creative ways to make them more vivid and relevant, while still preserving their original qualities and distinctive characteristics.
Có thể thấy rằng, để viết lại lịch sử là: It is clear that rewriting history has never been an easy task. Through exploration, research, experimentation and development, the people involved in the journey to revive Kim Hoang folk paintings have devoted immense passion, dedication, effort, time and financial resources to this endeavour.
